proposedTopics.title: viem clients: public, wallet & transports
proposedTopics.description: viem splits access into a Public Client (read-only: eth_call, getBalance, logs) and a Wallet Client (accounts, signing, and transactions), each built over a Transport (http, webSocket, or a custom EIP-1193 provider). You configure a chain and transport once and reuse the client. This separation makes it explicit which calls need wallet authority and which do not.

Done when: `getBalance` returns via the public client and the wallet client exposes an address from the injected provider, with the two responsibilities clearly separated.

proposedTopics.title: Reading contracts with viem
proposedTopics.description: readContract calls a view/pure function by supplying the contract address, ABI, function name, and args: it performs an eth_call rather than sending a transaction. Passing the ABI `as const` gives viem full type inference so return and argument types are checked at compile time. multicall batches compatible reads through Multicall3 in one RPC request.

proposedTopics.title: Writing transactions with viem & wagmi
proposedTopics.description: A useful write path is simulate-then-write: simulateContract validates the call against the state it reads and returns a prepared request; writeContract asks the account to sign and sends it, returning a hash to pass to waitForTransactionReceipt. In wagmi/React, useSimulateContract can compose with useWriteContract, then useWaitForTransactionReceipt tracks confirmation. Simulation reduces avoidable failures but cannot guarantee later execution against changed state.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in frontend/src/write.ts (or a wagmi component) simulate then write an ERC-20 transfer, then wait for the receipt and show status. Done when: a would-revert transfer is caught by simulateContract before any wallet prompt, and a valid transfer returns a mined receipt you display.

proposedTopics.title: Watching events & logs (viem)
proposedTopics.description: watchContractEvent watches new contract logs and invokes onLogs with decoded events; getContractEvents fetches historical logs over a block range. Applications must reconcile provisional UI state with confirmed chain state across reorgs.

proposedTopics.title: Sign-In With Ethereum (SIWE / EIP-4361)
proposedTopics.description: SIWE authenticates control of an address with a signed EIP-4361 message. The relying party must validate the signature and message fields relevant to the request, including domain, URI, chain ID, nonce, issued-at, and any validity bounds, then consume the server-issued nonce before starting a session. Contract accounts require ERC-1271-aware verification. A nonce alone is not the complete verification policy.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in frontend + a small server, implement SIWE: issue a single-use nonce, construct and sign the EIP-4361 message, then validate signature, domain, URI, chain ID, nonce, timestamps, and address before consuming the nonce and setting a session. Done when: a valid EOA login succeeds, wrong-origin/expired/replayed messages fail, and the verifier has an ERC-1271 path for contract accounts.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does viem split responsibilities between clients, and what is a Transport?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A Public Client does read-only calls (eth_call, getBalance, logs); a Wallet Client signs/sends (sendTransaction, signMessage); both sit over a Transport (http, webSocket, or injected EIP-1193). Pitfall: trying to sign with a public client (or read via a wallet client you didn't need a signer for) means you wired the wrong client — reads never need a signer.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does readContract need, and how do you get full type inference and fewer RPC calls?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: address + ABI + functionName + args; it is a decoded eth_call rather than a transaction. Declare an inline ABI `as const` so viem can infer argument and return types; use multicall for compatible reads in one RPC request. Pitfall: a widened ABI loses precise function and result inference.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why simulate before writeContract, and what's the wagmi hook trio?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: simulateContract validates against the state it reads and prepares a request before writeContract signs/sends; waitForTransactionReceipt tracks confirmation. In React, compose useSimulateContract with useWriteContract, then useWaitForTransactionReceipt. Pitfall: simulation reduces avoidable failures but cannot guarantee execution after state changes.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you get live vs historical events in viem, and what must you handle?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: watchContractEvent watches new decoded logs, normally polling a filter and falling back to getLogs; a WebSocket client can use subscriptions. getContractEvents fetches a historical range. Pitfall: a log-backed optimistic UI must reconcile against confirmed state after reorgs rather than treating the first callback as final.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does the wagmi CLI generate, and what class of bug does it eliminate?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: From your ABIs (Foundry/Hardhat artifacts or Etherscan) it generates fully-typed React hooks/actions, so a renamed function or wrong arg type is a compile error. Pitfall: forgetting to re-run `wagmi generate` after a contract change leaves stale types that compile but call a signature that no longer exists.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What interface does an injected wallet expose, and why does EIP-6963 exist?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An EIP-1193 provider with request({method,params}) and events like accountsChanged/chainChanged; EIP-6963 adds multi-wallet discovery so several extensions don't clobber window.ethereum. Pitfall: caching the account/chain once and never subscribing to the change events leaves your UI acting on a stale account after the user switches.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does WalletConnect add over an injected wallet, and what do RainbowKit/ConnectKit save you?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: WalletConnect links to mobile wallets over an encrypted relay session (QR/deep link), no extension needed; RainbowKit/ConnectKit are wagmi-based modals that handle injected + WalletConnect connectors, chain switching, and account UI out of the box. Pitfall: WalletConnect needs a valid projectId — omitting it silently breaks mobile connections.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does SIWE authenticate a user, and why is the nonce essential?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The user signs an EIP-4361 message; the server verifies the signature plus expected domain, URI, version, chain ID, address, nonce, issued-at, and any validity bounds before consuming the nonce and starting a session. EOAs use ERC-191 verification, while contract accounts need an ERC-1271 path on the specified chain. Pitfall: a valid signature and nonce alone do not make the message valid for this relying party.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Reading event logs on the frontend
proposedPrompts.promptText: How do indexed vs non-indexed event params affect querying, and why don't raw log queries scale?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Indexed params become searchable topics you can filter on (e.g. Transfers to an address); non-indexed params sit in the data field. Pitfall: RPCs cap block ranges and reorgs remove logs, so scanning full history from the client is slow and fragile — that's the reason to move to an indexer (The Graph/Ponder).

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the three parts of a subgraph, and what does it give the frontend?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A manifest (contracts/events to watch), a GraphQL schema (entities), and AssemblyScript mappings (event → entity updates); The Graph indexes it and serves a GraphQL API of clean, aggregated data. Pitfall: mappings only see data emitted in events — anything the contract never logged can't be indexed retroactively, so design your events for the queries you'll need.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Build and deploy a subgraph indexing an ERC-20's Transfer events into per-account entities.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Write the manifest + schema (Account, Transfer) + AssemblyScript mapping, then deploy to a local Graph node or Subgraph Studio and query balances via GraphQL.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Ponder differ from The Graph in language and operating model?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Ponder uses TypeScript indexing functions, backfills and live-syncs into Postgres, and exposes HTTP query APIs including generated GraphQL and SQL; you deploy the service. The Graph uses subgraph manifests, schemas, AssemblyScript mappings, and its network. Pitfall: self-hosting means you own indexer availability and operations.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the two Scaffold-ETH 2 packages, and what does the toolchain auto-generate?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A contracts package (Foundry/Hardhat) and a Next.js frontend pre-wired with wagmi/viem + RainbowKit; deployments generate a typed contract registry the UI reads, plus a burner wallet and an auto-rendered Debug Contracts page. Pitfall: the frontend's typed contract info comes from the deploy step — forgetting to redeploy leaves the UI pointing at an old address/ABI.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do the Scaffold hooks add over raw wagmi hooks?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: They resolve ABI/address from deployed contract info, so contractName + functionName drive typed reads, writeContractAsync submissions, and event history/watch hooks without raw wiring. Receipt tracking remains a separate concern. Pitfall: contracts absent from deployed or configured external contract data cannot be resolved by name.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete the current first Speedrun Ethereum challenge (Crowdfunding).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Implement CrowdFund.sol with contribute (payable), deadline + threshold, execute() to fund FundingRecipient or open refunds, and checks-effects-interactions withdraw; pass checkpoint tests and ship the contribution UI.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In the Crowdfunding challenge, why let contributors withdraw rather than pushing every refund?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Each contributor claims their recorded balance after an unsuccessful deadline, avoiding an unbounded refund loop and one recipient blocking everyone. Zero the balance before the external call. Pitfall: guard the state machine so contributions, successful execution, and refunds cannot overlap incorrectly.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does selling tokens back to the Vendor need a separate approve step?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: sellTokens uses transferFrom, which spends the user's ERC-20 allowance, so the user must first approve the Vendor to move their tokens; buying (payable ETH) needs no approval. Pitfall: forgetting the approve makes sellTokens revert with an allowance error — the classic first-dApp UX bug.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is the Dice Game's on-chain randomness exploitable?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: DiceGame hashes blockhash(block.number - 1), its own address, and a public nonce, then takes modulo 16. RiggedRoll reads the same inputs before calling and plays only for rolls 0–5. Pitfall: deterministic public inputs are predictable; use a VRF or a correctly designed commit-reveal when unpredictability is required.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete SpeedRunEthereum Challenge 3 (Dice Game / RiggedRoll).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Write RiggedRoll to recompute DiceGame's predictable roll and call rollTheDice only on a winning prediction (funding the contract to pay the fee); pass the challenge tests.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete SpeedRunEthereum Challenge 4 (Build a DEX).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Implement init liquidity, price via x*y=k with a 0.3% fee, ethToToken/tokenToEth swaps, and deposit/withdraw of LP shares; build a swap UI showing reserves and expected output.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In the DEX challenge, how is the output of a swap priced?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The challenge sets inputWithFee = input * 997, then output = (inputWithFee * outputReserve) / (inputReserve * 1000 + inputWithFee). Pitfall: a spot-price quote ignores slippage, and swap functions without a minimum output expose users to sandwiching.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Speedrun: later challenges (Multisig, SVG NFT, Oracle)
proposedPrompts.promptText: How do the three oracle designs in the current challenge trade trust for complexity?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The whitelist oracle trusts approved reporters; the staking oracle decentralizes reporting with stake, rewards, inactivity penalties, and slashing; the optimistic oracle accepts bonded proposals unless disputed, then a decider settles the outcome. Pitfall: each design moves trust rather than eliminating it, so state the authority, incentives, latency, and dispute assumptions.
